title: Tibetan Ice May Preserve the Last Ice Age
paragraphs: Scientists studied ice from the Guliya ice cap, a large area of ice on a high plateau in northwest Tibet. Their study was published in the journal Science Advances.

The team took ice cores in 1992 and again in 2015. A core is a long piece of ice taken from deep inside a glacier. Both cores had very similar patterns in a chemical signal called oxygen isotopes, so the results seem reliable.

Earlier work said the ice only went back about 12,000 years. Now the scientists think some of it may be more than 128,000 years old. If they are right, the ice keeps a record of the last ice age. They plan to test more samples to learn more.

questions.q: What did the two cores have in common?
questions.a: They showed very similar oxygen isotope patterns.
